newsitem.title: USA: HK leaders reject linkage of trade and human rights.
newsitem.headline: HK leaders reject linkage of trade and human rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's leaders have warned Republicans in the U.S. Congress that their proposals to use trade privileges as leverage to protect human rights in the territory would threaten its economic livelihood, the Washington Post reported on Friday.

In letters sent this week to House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and other Republican lawmakers, Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten hailed as "extremely welcome" congressional support for the preservation of civil liberties in Hong Kong after its July 1 handover from Britain to China.
But the newspaper said Patten strenuously objected to the proposals, backed by Gingrich, to renew China's trading privileges for less than a full year to maintain pressure on Beijing on the issue.

Such proposals "would jeopardize rather than reinforce (Hong Kong's) way of life," Patten said, because uncertainty over U.S.-China trade would inflict a serious blow on the economy of Hong Kong, a major gateway for China's global commerce.
"For the people of Hong Kong there is no comfort in the proposition that if China reduces their freedoms the United States will take away their jobs," Patten wrote, according to the Post.
The newspaper said Hong Kong business leaders and government officials visiting Washington this week expressed sentiments similar to Patten's.

Gingrich said on April 30 that a six-month extension of China's Most Favored Nation (MFN) trading status -- instead of the one-year extensions that have been approved in the past -- would be an "appropriate ...signal" to underscore U.S. concern over whether China will permit Hong Kong to maintain its freedoms.
The Post said Republican leaders were reassessing their plans in light of Hong Kong's complaint and similar objections from U.S. business executives.
